intro: Martha Goldstein plays an 1851 Érard in this étude of awkward little clashes and a generous E-major song. Chopin asks the same piano to joke in short, broken phrases and then sing like a cello.

sections.label: A · E minor, joking in semitones
sections.mNote: Light broken chords brush against neighbouring notes

sections.label: B · A cello-like song in E major
sections.mNote: The low melody sings beneath flowing right-hand figures

sections.label: C · The clipped E-minor tune returns
sections.mNote: The opening’s quick clashes and broken rhythms return

sections.label: Coda · Full chords and an upward flourish
sections.mNote: Fortissimo chords lead to the E-major close

cues.title: An Érard from 1851
cues.text: Goldstein’s piano is an Érard built in 1851, two years after Chopin’s death. The recording comes from her survey of the études for Pandora Records, preserved in the Al Goldstein collection.
cues.evidence: Pandora PAN 107 credits Martha Goldstein and an Érard piano dated 1851. The recording date is unlisted. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Frederic_Chopin_-_Opus_25_-_Twelve_Grand_Etudes_-_e_minor.ogg

cues.title: A cello inside the piano
cues.text: The middle section changes to E major and Più lento. Its melody lies low, where a cello might sing, while the right hand supplies rising and falling figures. Chopin writes long phrases here after the opening’s clipped semitone clashes.
cues.evidence: Mieczysław Tomaszewski describes the low melody and figuration at https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191. E-major Più lento: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the short phrases
cues.text: The E-minor tune returns with its quick dissonances. Chopin’s scherzando writing flicks between broken chords and short replies. The same hands that carried the middle song now have to release each little gesture quickly.
cues.evidence: Outer sections marked Vivace, scherzando and leggiero; broken rhythm and guitar-like arpeggios described by Tomaszewski. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Érard’s last chords
cues.text: The close expands into fortissimo chords and an upward flourish in E major. The right hand’s final G♯ hangs high above the bass.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski describes the final dramatic turn, fortissimo chords and ascending major-key flourish at https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191. Final G♯: Fred Yu, https://www.ourchopin.com/analysis/etude25.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
